finding: The interviews do not establish reduced readmission, infection cure, treatment retention, mortality benefit or causal effectiveness of the SIRI team.
The study does not demonstrate that the network improved equity, cancer outcomes or population access, or that its model transfers to public safety.
The study does not establish uptake, analytical accuracy, behavior change, overdose prevention or effectiveness of a service not yet operational.
The cross-sectional unadjusted comparisons do not show that courses caused higher knowledge, validate the proprietary test, measure practical competence or predict patient outcomes.
It cannot establish any public-health, policing, economic or causal effect because outcomes have not yet been reported.
The study does not estimate how often EMS is avoided, quantify police effects, establish overdose outcomes or represent people outside participating harm-reduction sites.
It does not demonstrate that CFIR, EPIS or any implementation strategy improves policing outcomes, legitimacy, safety or sustainability.
The uncontrolled evaluation and modeled scenarios do not establish causal clinical benefit, mortality reduction, realized regional savings or superiority over alternative systems.
The survey does not establish prevalence across US policing, causal determinants of implementation success, innovation effectiveness or transferability to Brazil.

The study does not establish improved officer behavior, public safety, accountability, technology accuracy or general effects across agencies; department assignment was not randomized for this comparison.
